draft.draft_body: {"type":"doc","content":[{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"There is an old question about God and suffering, and it has never gone away. It goes like this. If God is willing to stop evil but cannot, then God is not all-powerful. If God can stop evil but will not, then God is not good. And if God is both willing and able, then why does evil exist? Every way you turn it, the answer fails."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The question only works against a particular idea of God. The idea that God is one being among many, with power and a will, able to step in and stop things. Advaita Vedanta does not answer that question. It questions the frame itself. And that is not a trick. It is the heart of the teaching."}]},{"type":"captionedImage","content":[{"type":"image2","attrs":{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b5ddc305-5f12-4f51-aeb2-bb78d67431e0_1200x560.png","alt":"Why evil exists, and the frame we ask it in"}},{"type":"caption","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The question assumes God and evil are two things in the same world. The old teaching asks what world that is."}]}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The question assumes two separate things"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The old question assumes God sits next to evil, in the same world, and we ask why God allows it. Nearly every answer in the West tries to explain it that way. Some say evil comes from human free will, so God is not to blame. Some say you cannot have light without dark. Some say suffering makes us stronger. Each answer is a real attempt. Each one keeps God and evil in the same frame, arguing."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Advaita lets go of that frame. In Advaita, the deepest reality, called Brahman, is not one being among many. It is not more powerful or more good than other things. It is beyond good and evil, beyond every pair of opposites. It is not the kind of thing that could step in, because it is not a thing."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Evil is not a thing. It is a mistaken way of seeing."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Advaita does not start with God. It starts with us. The world we see, full of sharp separations, of good and evil, of self and other, is not the last word. It is how the world looks when we see it wrongly. The old teaching calls this Maya, the power of appearance."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"There is a story that makes this plain. In dim light, you see a rope on the ground and your mind reads it as a snake. Your heart pounds. You step back. But there was never a snake. There was only a rope you misread. The fear was real. The snake was not."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Evil is like that. It is real as an experience, and it is not a thing in itself. When we see ourselves as separate from everything else, we act only for ourselves, and that is where what we call evil comes from. The evil is not a force opposing God. It is what happens when we misread who we are."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"The answer is not a fix. It is a seeing."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"If evil is a mistaken way of seeing, then the answer is not to fix it from outside. It is to see rightly. Advaita says your real self, called Atman, is the same as Brahman, the deepest reality. When you see that, the sharp line between good and evil, between you and the world, starts to soften."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The goal is called Moksha, which means freedom. It is not winning a fight against evil. It is the end of the confusion that made the fight seem real. Moksha is not a reward for being good. It is waking up from the mistake."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"This is not the same as saying suffering does not hurt. Suffering is real. War is real. Cruelty is real. The loss of someone you love is real. No honest person in this tradition would tell you otherwise. The point is narrower and stranger: these things are real as experiences, and they are not the last word about what the world is. The rope was always a rope. The fear was still real."}]},{"type":"heading","attrs":{"level":2},"content":[{"type":"text","text":"Why the difference matters"}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The question about God and evil is a real question, and it deserves a real answer. Advaita is not saying the question is silly. It is saying the question is asked from inside a way of seeing that the teaching says we can wake from. That is a different kind of answer. Not a solution to the puzzle, but a way to see the puzzle itself more clearly."}]},{"type":"paragraph","content":[{"type":"text","text":"Some questions are not answered. They are outgrown. This may be one of them. It is not that we stop asking. It is that we ask from a different place."}]}]}
